findings.title: Double dependency graph evaluation per frame step
findings.description: step_frame() at line 388 calls sync_scene_to_solver(scene, sess) without forwarding the depsgraph parameter. sync_scene_to_solver (line 378) defaults depsgraph=None, which causes gather_colliders (line 269) to call bpy.context.evaluated_depsgraph_get() — a full dependency graph rebuild — unconditionally. Meanwhile, the frame-change handler _on_frame_change (line 458) already calls sync_scene_to_solver(scene, sess, depsgraph) with the handler-supplied depsgraph BEFORE calling step_frame. This means gather_colliders runs TWICE per frame: once with the correct depsgraph from the handler, and once triggering a fresh eval from inside step_frame. Each call creates new wp.Mesh objects and re-reads evaluated mesh data.
findings.impact: Per-frame CPU time doubled for collider-heavy scenes; unnecessary GPU memory allocations from orphaned wp.Mesh objects; risk of stutter during interactive playback as the depsgraph is rebuilt redundantly each frame.
findings.fix: Forward the depsgraph through step_frame or cache it on the Session. Either (a) add optional depsgraph param to step_frame and pass it through to sync_scene_to_solver, or (b) cache the depsgraph reference on the Session during _on_frame_change and reuse it in step_frame.

findings.title: Uncached wp.Mesh creation per frame for all colliders
findings.description: gather_colliders() at line 282-302 evaluates every COLLIDER-tagged Blender mesh to a new wp.Mesh on every frame, even for static colliders whose transforms and topology have not changed. The mesh is reconstructed from mesh.vertices and mesh.loop_triangles, copied to a GPU wp.array, and wrapped in a new wp.Mesh instance. The old ColliderDesc objects (with their wp.Mesh references) are discarded by set_colliders(). Each frame the GPU pipeline allocates and uploads geometry for every collider, even when nothing changed.
findings.impact: Unnecessary GPU upload bandwidth and allocation churn. For scenes with multiple high-resolution collider meshes, this can cause frame-time spikes and GPU memory fragmentation. The problem compounds with EE-001 (double evaluation), doubling the waste.
findings.fix: Cache the wp.Mesh keyed by (object name, object matrix hash, mesh geometry hash). Only rebuild when the source mesh topology or world transform has changed. Store the cache on the Session object.

findings.title: Object velocity miscomputed during timeline scrubbing
findings.description: _object_velocity() at line 197 computes velocity as v = (cur - prev) / dt where dt = (frame - prev_frame) / fps. During normal frame-by-frame playback, dt = 1/fps and the velocity is correct. But when the user scrubs the timeline (e.g., jump from frame 1 to frame 100), the stored prev_frame was from frame 1 but the new cur is at frame 100, giving dt = 99/fps. This produces a velocity ~99x smaller than the true single-frame velocity, making moving colliders appear nearly stationary during scrubbing. The stale velocity is then applied to the pressure solve and collision response for that sim step.
findings.impact: Collider-driven fluid motion (e.g., a moving paddle or搅拌器) receives incorrect impulse during timeline scrubbing. The fluid appears to pass through or fail to react to fast-moving colliders. The incorrect velocity is committed into the sim state and persists into subsequent frames.
findings.fix: Compute per-frame velocity from the difference between the current frame and the previous sim-step frame, not the previous display frame. Alternatively, track velocity independently from frame count by storing the previous world-space position and computing v = (cur - prev) / (time_step) where time_step is the actual solver timestep used, capped to a maximum expected dt.

findings.title: Silent swallow of simulation step exceptions during playback
findings.description: The frame-change handler _on_frame_change() at line 460 catches all exceptions from sync_scene_to_solver and step_frame and suppresses them: the exception is printed to the console and stored in sess.error, and fs.status is set to an error message string. No Blender UI notification (self.report) is raised because the handler is not an operator — it's a frame_change_post handler. Subsequent frame changes will keep trying to step, each time failing and printing another error. The user sees only the stale status text and must know to check the console.
findings.impact: Silent simulation failure during interactive playback. The solver enters an error state but playback continues; the user may not notice until checking the console or seeing frozen output. Frame-change handlers that throw repeatedly can also degrade Blender responsiveness.
findings.fix: After the first error, set a flag on the Session (e.g., sess.error_state = True) and check it at the top of _on_frame_change to skip further stepping until the user explicitly resets or reinitializes. Optionally print a one-time prominent warning. Also call bpy.ops.wm.redraw_timer() to force a status bar update so the error message is visible.

findings.title: Irreversible sim lag during frame-skipped playback
findings.description: In step_frame() (line 388) and the frame-change handler (line 441), the simulation advances exactly one step per frame_change_post event regardless of how many display frames were skipped. The handler sets sess.last_frame to the current display frame (line 456), not the sim frame. If Blender drops frames or the user scrubs from frame 1 to frame 100, only one sim step executes. The sim then permanently lags behind display — it never catches up because subsequent events each advance by exactly 1 regardless of the gap. This is a design trade-off for interactivity (line 454 comment), but the sim-offset accumulates without bound during scrubbing or dropped frames.
findings.impact: After a timeline scrub or frame skip, the simulated fluid state diverges from the expected display-frame correspondence. Exported frame data and cached frames correspond to a different timeline position than the Blender frame number suggests. The offset is never recovered.
findings.fix: Advance the sim by multiple substep batches to close the gap, with a configurable max catch-up (e.g., at most 4 sim steps per frame event). Or maintain a separate sim frame counter that increments by the actual number of substeps and only use display frame for UI display purposes.

findings.title: sys.modules leak across snippet recompilation
findings.description: CompiledSnippet._compile() (line 234-249) generates a unique module name from a SHA1 hash of the kernel source. Each time the user edits a snippet and clicks Apply, a new module is added to sys.modules. The old modules with different source hashes remain in sys.modules forever — there is no cleanup mechanism. The _compile() method checks for existing modules (line 243) and reuses them if found (cache hit), but a replacement snippet with different code generates an entirely new module entry. Over many edit-compile cycles, sys.modules accumulates stale module objects.
findings.impact: Slow memory leak in the Python process. Each compiled Warp kernel module retains its generated source code, compiled bytecode, and references to the imported Warp module. Over hundreds of snippet edits, this can consume tens of megabytes of Python heap that is never reclaimed.
findings.fix: Track previously loaded snippet module names per kernel_name and explicitly delete old entries from sys.modules before inserting new ones. Add a bounded LRU cache keyed on (kernel_name, source_hash) instead of unbounded accumulation by source_hash alone. Alternatively, clean up by kernel_name at the start of set_snippets().

findings.title: Shared _collider_prev dict collision risk between sources and colliders
findings.description: The Session._collider_prev dictionary (line 32) is shared between gather_sources() and gather_colliders(), both of which call _object_velocity(). The key is obj.name, which is unique within a Blender scene for mesh objects. However, if the same object is tagged as both a SOURCE and a COLLIDER (possible via UI), each call to _object_velocity from the different gather functions overwrites the other's prev state. Additionally, if an object is renamed between frames, the old name key persists in the dictionary as a leaked entry with no cleanup.
findings.impact: If an object is dual-tagged, both roles share a single velocity state entry, causing one role to see the velocity from the other's frame timing. Old- name entries accumulate over time if objects are frequently renamed, representing a minor memory leak.
findings.fix: Qualify the dict keys by role (e.g., ('src:' + obj.name) and ('col:' + obj.name)). Add cleanup: either periodically sweep keys whose objects no longer exist in the scene, or clear and rebuild the dict each frame based on current scene objects.

findings.title: Simulation reset silently overwrites previously cached frames
findings.description: The cache write_frame() function (line 30) uses solver.frame as the frame number in the cache filename (fluidsim_XXXXX.npz). When reset_simulation() is called, solver.frame resets to 0 from FluidSolver.reset(). If the user then re-runs the simulation from frame 1, cached files from the previous run at the same sim frame numbers are silently overwritten by np.savez_compressed. Additionally, there is no atomic write pattern — a crash during np.savez_compressed leaves a partial .npz file that read_frame() will try to load and fail on.
findings.impact: Loss of previously cached simulation data after a reset. Partial .npz files cause crashes on reload (np.load will raise an exception on a truncated archive). Users relying on cached frames for offline rendering may lose data without warning.
findings.fix: Include a run-ID or timestamp in the cache path to differentiate runs. Write to a temporary file and atomic-rename to the final path to prevent partial writes. Use np.load with mmap_mode=None inside a try/except in read_frame() to handle corrupted files gracefully.

findings.title: GPU device state not validated before Toggle Live activation
findings.description: FLUIDSIM_OT_toggle_live.execute() at line 107 checks bridge.session().active (which tests solver is not None) but does not verify the GPU device is still in a valid state. If the GPU driver was reset, the Warp device context was lost, or the CUDA context was invalidated between initialization and toggle_live, sess.active returns True but any subsequent kernel launch will fail with a device error. The error will be caught by _on_frame_change's exception handler, but by then the user has already toggled live mode and may not understand why playback silently fails.
findings.impact: Misleading 'Solver ready' status when the GPU state is actually invalid. User enables live playback expecting simulation but gets no visible output and an opaque console error.
findings.fix: Add a lightweight GPU health check before setting fs.live = True. For example, launch a trivial Warp kernel (e.g., wp.launch a no-op kernel with dim=1) and catch device errors. If the device is stale, force reinitialization from the current scene before activating live mode.

findings.title: No recovery path for grid topology allocation failure
findings.description: FluidSolver._rebuild_topology() at line 615 calls g.finalize_topology() which allocates new GPU leaf arrays. If this GPU allocation fails (OOM, device lost, TDR), the exception propagates up through step_frame() to the caller. The solver is left in an inconsistent state: self.grid has an incomplete topology, self.old_leaf_table was already overwritten via wp.copy at line 595, and the churn data buffer swap (line 624) may be skipped, leaving churn.data pointing to an undersized array.
findings.impact: An OOM mid-simulation leaves the solver in a corrupted state from which the only recovery is release + reinitialize. Any subsequent operation on the solver (step, surface extraction, particle readback) will either crash or produce garbage.
findings.fix: Wrap _rebuild_topology() in step_frame() with a try/except that resets the solver to a safe state on failure (e.g., force a full reset via self.reset() and set an error flag on the stats object). Alternatively, pre-allocate a worst-case grid capacity at init and avoid runtime topology reallocation.
